name: NJ-12
label: Safe D

key_factors: District's strong Democratic lean (D+13 PVI) persists with the open seat
Hamawy's roughly $1.9 million raised plus matching outside support versus Mele's $96,000
Prediction markets price the Democratic side near 97 percent
No public general-election polling, leaving the outlook reliant on fundamentals
model.rationale: The district's thirteen-point Democratic lean, Hamawy's roughly twenty-to-one fundraising and outside-spending advantage, and market pricing near 97 percent all point to a comfortable Democratic hold despite the open seat. With no polls available, the fundamentals carry the forecast, and they point the same direction.
model.watch: A late wave of outside spending for Mele or an unusually favorable Republican turnout environment could narrow the margin, though flipping the outcome would require a far larger shift.
notes: No expert rater lists this race; treated as safe for the party holding the seat.
No usable general-election polls; forecast rests on fundamentals and expert ratings.
Open seat: Bonnie Watson Coleman (D) is not on the ballot.

overview:
New Jersey's 12th district has leaned Democratic by about thirteen points in recent elections, and Bonnie Watson Coleman's retirement does not put the seat seriously in play. Democrat Adam Hamawy has raised roughly $1.9 million and drawn nearly as much in outside support, while Republican Gregg Mele has raised under $100,000 with little outside help. Prediction markets put Democratic odds near 97 percent.

No public polls cover the general election, so the outlook rests on district fundamentals and the money gap. A Green and an independent candidate are on the ballot but lack resources. The seat remains solidly Democratic, with the main uncertainty being the size of the margin rather than the winner.
